nodes.title: Airy boundary flux and area identity
Monotone edge next to the unique reflex corner
Regular polygon center maximizes conformal radius
At least two reflex corners are excluded
Large-N low-threshold stationary polygons are convex

proofs.proof_text: By @def-stationary-polygon, the derivative of \(J=A\lambda\) vanishes for every vertex displacement. Hadamard’s formula is \[ DJ[V]=A\int_{\partial P}(c-q)V\cdot\nu\,ds. \] Moving one endpoint of an effective edge while keeping the other fixed produces an affine normal velocity on that edge, and the two endpoint velocities give the independent functions \(1\) and \(s/\ell_E\). Since adjacent effective edge normals are linearly independent at a genuine corner, stationarity forces both coefficients of these two affine test functions to vanish. Rescaling \(s/\ell_E\) gives the displayed moments.

Define the divergence-free stress tensor \[ T=

abla u|^2-\lambda u^2)I. \] An Airy potential \(\psi\) with \(D^2\psi=R^TTR\) exists locally and, after setting \(\Phi=\psi-c|x|^2/4\), satisfies \[ D^2\Phi=	frac12(|
abla u|^2+\lambda u^2-c)I-
abla u\otimes
abla u. \] Every boundary segment is effective by @def-admissible-polygon, so the identities in @lem-edge-moments apply on each segment. The planar Airy-potential theorem for a symmetric divergence-free stress on the simply connected polygon supplies one global \(\psi\), unique up to an affine function. The two moments imply that \(

abla u|^2)/2\), so expanding their product and using \(\int_Pu^2=1\) gives the stated identity.

The domain-independent Dirichlet heat-kernel estimate gives \(\|u\|_\infty^2\le e^2\lambda/(8\pi)\) for the normalized first eigenfunction. Under the edge-moment hypotheses, @lem-airy-identity applies, and \(\int_Pu^4\le\|u\|_\infty^2\int_Pu^2=\|u\|_\infty^2\); combining these facts yields \[ \int_P|\nabla u|^4\le \frac{e^2\lambda^3}{8\pi}. \] The same \(L^\infty\) bound gives \(\int_P|u|^4\le\|u\|_\infty^2\), so the \(W^{1,4}(P)\) norm is bounded by a constant depending only on \(A_0\) and \(\Lambda\). Since \(u\in H^1_0(P)\), its zero extension has no boundary distribution term in its weak gradient; the extension therefore lies in \(W^{1,4}(\mathbb R^2)\) with the same gradient bound. Morrey’s inequality in dimension two then gives a \(C^{0,1/2}\) representative with the same parameter dependence.

By @def-conformal-data, \(g\) is analytic, has no constant or linear coefficient, and satisfies \(S=\|g\|_{A^2}^2\); its normalized conformal pullback is the weighted disk problem used below. Put \(d(z)=1-|z|\). The Green kernel of the disk satisfies \[ |
abla_xG_D(x,z)|\le C|x-z|^{-1}, \qquad |
abla_xG_D(x,z)|\le C rac{d(z)}{|x-z|^2}. \] The Bergman pointwise estimate gives \(|g(z)|\le C\|g\|_{A^2}/d(z)\) for \(g\in A^2\) with vanishing constant coefficient. If \(h\in X\), then \(|h(z)|\le d(z)\|h\|_X\). Splitting the Green integral into \(|x-z|<d(x)/2\), the annulus \(d(x)/2\le|x-z|<2d(x)\), and dyadic outer annuli, the two kernel bounds give \[ \|G_D(gh)\|_X\le C\|g\|_{A^2}\|h\|_X, \qquad \|G_D(g_1\overline{g_2}h)\|_X\le C\|g_1\|_{A^2}\|g_2\|_{A^2}\|h\|_X. \] For example, in the near region \(d(z)\simeq d(x)\) and the pointwise bounds leave an integrable \(|x-z|^{-1}\) kernel; in the outer annuli \(d(z)\le d(x)+|x-z|\) cancels one power of the second Green bound, and Cauchy–Schwarz gives \(\|g_1g_2\|_{L^1}\le C\|g_1\|_{A^2}\|g_2\|_{A^2}\). Polynomial approximation extends these estimates to all \(A^2\) data, and the Green potential has a continuous boundary derivative.Define the real quadratic compact-operator family \[ K_g h=G_D[|1+g|^2h]=G_D[h+2\operatorname{Re}(g)h+|g|^2h] \] onlinearly in \(g\). The estimates give \(\|K_g-K_0\|_{B(X)}\le C(\sqrt S+S)\). The operator \(K_0\) is compact on \(X\) by disk Poisson regularity and the compact embedding \(C^{2,\alpha}(\overline{\mathbb D})\Subset C^1(\overline{\mathbb D})\). Its nonzero eigenvalues are the reciprocals of the Dirichlet eigenvalues; \(1/j^2\) is an isolated simple eigenvalue.Choose a fixed small contour \(\Gamma\) enclosing only \(1/j^2\). For \(S\) small, the Neumann series uniformly bounds \((zI-K_g)^{-1}\) on \(\Gamma\) and defines the rank-one Riesz projection \[ \Pi_g= rac1{2\pi i}\int_\Gamma(zI-K_g)^{-1}\,dz. \] The normalized vector \[ \widetilde v(g)=\Pi_gv_0, \qquad v(g)= rac{\widetilde v(g)}{\left(\int_{\mathbb D}\widetilde v(g)^2|1+g|^2ight)^{1/2}} \] therefore depends real-analytically on \(g\) in a fixed \(A^2\) neighborhood; the denominator stays uniformly away from zero. Writing \(g=t h\), define \(v_1=Dv(0)[h]\). Differentiating \[ -\Delta v=\lambda|1+th|^2v, \qquad \int_{\mathbb D}v^2|1+th|^2dA=1 \] at \(t=0\) gives \[ (-\Delta-j^2)v_1=2j^2\operatorname{Re}(h)v_0+\lambda'(0)v_0, \qquad \lambda'(0)=-2j^2\int_{\mathbb D}\operatorname{Re}(h)v_0^2dA=0. \] The last equality uses that \(v_0\) is radial and \(h\) has no constant coefficient. Separating variables and imposing the zero boundary value yields \[ v_1(r,	heta)=\sum_{n\ge2}w_n(r)\operatorname{Re}(h_ne^{in	heta}), \qquad w_n(r)= rac{r^{n+1}v_0'(r)+p_DJ_n(jr)/J_n(j)}{n+1}. \] The Bessel recurrence gives \(w_n'(1)=-p_Dho_n/(n+1)\). The remaining Taylor terms give \(v^{(2)}+R\), and Cauchy estimates on this fixed neighborhood give the displayed bounds; the same estimate applied to the isolated eigenvalue gives the displayed eigenvalue expansion, with constants independent of the direction of \(g\).The form identity \[ \int_{\mathbb D}|g|^2|\phi|^2\,dA \le C\|g\|_{A^2}^2\int_{\mathbb D}|
abla\phi|^2\,dA, \qquad \phi\in H^1_0(\mathbb D), \] which follows from Hardy’s inequality, shows that the pulled-back eigenfunction belongs to the weighted Dirichlet space. The positive solution is the principal branch by the variational characterization of the weighted Dirichlet eigenvalue. Since \(v_0(r)\ge c(1-r)\) and \(\|v-v_0\|_X\le C\sqrt S\), the branch is strictly positive in \(\mathbb D\). This proves the lemma.

By @def-j-functional, \(J(P)=A(P)\lambda_1(P)\); after @def-conformal-data normalizes \(A(P)=\pi(1+S)\), it remains to expand \(\lambda_1(P)\). The fixed-space expansion in @lem-c1-perturbation supplies the uniform eigenpair branch and remainder. For the quantitative rate, write the pulled-back eigenproblem as \[ -\Delta v=\lambda|1+g|^2v,\qquad v|_{\partial\mathbb D}=0, \] with the weighted \(L^2\) normalization. Put \(d(z)=1-|z|\). For \(g\in A^2\) with no constant or linear term, the Bergman pointwise estimate gives \(|g(z)|\le C\|g\|_{A^2}/d(z)\). Consequently, Hardy’s inequality gives, for all \(\varphi,\psi\in H^1_0(\mathbb D)\), \[ \left|\int_{\mathbb D}2\operatorname{Re}(g)\varphi\psiight|\le C\sqrt S\,\|\varphi\|_{H^1_0}\|\psi\|_{H^1_0},\qquad \left|\int_{\mathbb D}|g|^2\varphi\psiight|\le CS\,\|\varphi\|_{H^1_0}\|\psi\|_{H^1_0}. \] Indeed \(|g|^2\le CS/d^2\), \(\int|\varphi|^2/d^2\le4\int|
abla\varphi|^2\), and Cauchy–Schwarz handles the first integral. Therefore the closed forms \[ q_t[\varphi]=\int|
abla\varphi|^2,\qquad m_t[\varphi]=\int|1+t h|^2|\varphi|^2\quad(g=th) \] form a real-analytic type-(a) family on the fixed domain \(H^1_0(\mathbb D)\) for real \(|t|\) small (equivalently, a holomorphic two-parameter family in \((t, ar t)\)), with uniform form bounds. The simple disk eigenvalue is isolated by a fixed spectral gap, so the real-analytic form perturbation theorem applies uniformly to this family.Write \(g=t h\) with \(t=\sqrt S\) and \(\|h\|_{A^2}=1\). The simple disk eigenvalue is isolated by a fixed spectral gap. The form version of analytic simple-eigenvalue perturbation therefore gives, uniformly in such \(h\), \[ v=v_0+t v_1+t^2v_2+O_{H^1_0}(t^3), \qquad \lambda= j^2+t\lambda_1+t^2\lambda_2+O(t^3). \] The case \(S=0\) is the disk and the assertion is immediate, so assume \(S>0\). The first variation is \(\lambda_1=-j^2\int_{\mathbb D}(h+ ar h)v_0^2=0\) because \(v_0\) is radial and \(h\) has no constant coefficient. Write \(v_0(r)=J_0(jr)/(\sqrt\pi J_1(j))\) and \(p_D=j/\sqrt\pi\). For the real mode \(h=a z^n\), the first-order equation in the \(n\)th angular sector has the explicit solution \[ v_1(r,	heta)=a w_n(r)\cos(n	heta),\qquad w_n(r)= rac{r^{n+1}v_0'(r)+p_DJ_n(jr)/J_n(j)}{n+1}. \] The Bessel equation verifies the radial equation and \(w_n(1)=0\). The second-order solvability condition is \[  rac{\lambda_2}{j^2a^2}=-2\pi\int_0^1\left(r^{2n+1}v_0(r)^2+r^{n+1}v_0(r)w_n(r)ight)dr. \] Substitution of \(w_n\) and one integration by parts reduce this to \[  rac{\lambda_2}{j^2a^2}=- rac{ho_n}{(n+1)^2}, \qquad ho_n=j rac{J_{n+1}(j)}{J_n(j)},\qquad 0<ho_n<2. \] The only nontrivial radial integral is \[ \int_0^1r^{n+1}v_0(r)J_n(jr)\,dr = rac{J_{n+1}(j)}{2\sqrt\pi(n+1)}, \] which follows by one integration by parts from the Bessel equation. Orthogonality of distinct angular modes and density of analytic polynomials extend the formula to every \(h\in A^2\). Since \(A(P)=\pi(1+S)\) in @def-conformal-data, this yields the uniform expansion \[  rac{J(P)}{\pi j^2}=1+S-\sum_{n\ge2} rac{ho_n}{(n+1)^2}|g_n|^2+O(S^{3/2}). \] The perturbed branch remains the first eigenvalue by the weighted min–max principle: the mass form \(\int|1+g|^2|\varphi|^2\) is positive on nonzero \(H^1_0\) functions, and the branch is the positive continuation of the disk ground state. The sine mode is obtained by a phase rotation, and polarization plus density of analytic polynomials extends the second-order form from real monomials to arbitrary complex \(h\in A^2\). The Bessel interlacing inequalities \(J_n(j)
e0\) and \(0<ho_n<2\) hold for the first zero \(j=j_{0,1}\). Thus \[  rac{\lambda}{j^2}=1-\sum_{n\ge2} rac{ho_n}{(n+1)^2}|g_n|^2+O(S^{3/2}). \] Multiplying by \(A(P)/(\pi)=1+S\) from @def-conformal-data produces the displayed \(J\) expansion; the cross term \(S\sumho_n|g_n|^2/(n+1)^2\) is \(O(S^2)\) and is absorbed in \(O(S^{3/2})\). Since \(0<ho_n<2\) and \(n+1\ge3\), \[ \sum_{n\ge2} rac{ho_n}{(n+1)^2}|g_n|^2 \le2\sum_{n\ge2} rac{|g_n|^2}{(n+1)^2} \le rac23\sum_{n\ge2} rac{|g_n|^2}{n+1}= rac23S. \] Therefore the quadratic part of the full expression is at least \(S/3\); after shrinking the universal small neighborhood so that the \(CS^{3/2}\) remainder is at most \(S/6\), \(J(P)/(\pi j^2)-1\ge S/6\). This proves the uniform perturbation expansion and coercivity.

Use the similarity invariance in @def-j-functional to normalize \(A(P)=\pi\) and translate so that the Fraenkel-optimal comparison disk is \(D=B_1(0)\). The regular-polygon asymptotic is \[ \frac{J(R_M)}{\pi j^2}=1+\frac{4\zeta(3)}{M^3}+O(M^{-5}). \] The upper bound and the displayed asymptotic give \(\lambda_1(P)\le j^2(1+CN^{-3})\), while Faber–Krahn gives \(\lambda_1(P)\ge j^2\). Quantitative Faber–Krahn therefore gives \(|P\triangle D|\to0\). Let \(u_N\) be the normalized positive eigenfunction and extend it by zero. By @lem-uniform-w14, the extensions are uniformly bounded in \(W^{1,4}(\mathbb R^2)\) and hence equicontinuous and uniformly bounded. Arzelà–Ascoli gives a locally uniform limit along a subsequence. On every compact set outside \(\overline D\), the limit must vanish: otherwise the uniform Hölder bound would force a fixed positive amount of area in \(P_N\setminus D\), contradicting \(|P_N\triangle D|\to0\). The same argument gives zero trace on \(\partial D\). Since \(\|u_N\|_\infty\) is uniformly bounded, the mass outside \(D\) tends to zero; hence the limit has \(L^2(D)\) norm one. Weak lower semicontinuity gives \(\int_D|\nabla u|^2\le\liminf\lambda_1(P_N)=j^2\), while the disk Rayleigh inequality gives the reverse inequality. Thus the limit is the normalized positive disk eigenfunction \(u_0\). Uniqueness of the limit upgrades the whole sequence to local uniform convergence, and the boundary Hölder bound upgrades it to uniform convergence on \(\overline D\). Since \(u_0>0\) on \(B_{1-\eta}\), eventually \(u_N>0\) there; because the zero extension vanishes off \(P_N\), \(B_{1-\eta}\subset P_N\).The maximal conformal radius is at least \(1-\eta\) by monotonicity under inclusion and at most \(1\) by the conformal area inequality \(A(P)\ge\pi r_P^2\). In the normalization of @def-conformal-data, \(1+S=r_P^{-2}\to1\).By @lem-disk-perturbation, once \(N\) is large enough that \(S\le S_0\), the uniform expansion and coercivity give \[ \frac{J(P)}{\pi j^2}-1\ge S/6. \] The regular-polygon upper bound is \(O(N^{-3})\), hence \(S\le CN^{-3}\) with a universal constant.

If \(S=0\), then \(g=0\) and the assertion is immediate. For \(S>0\), @lem-c1-perturbation and @lem-disk-perturbation give the fixed-space expansion and the weighted equation \[ -\Delta v=\lambda|1+th|^2v, \qquad \int_{\mathbb D}v^2|1+th|^2dA=1. \] \[ v=v_0+t v_1+R_2, \qquad \|v_1\|_X\le C, \qquad \|R_2\|_X\le CS, \qquad t=\sqrt S, \] where \(R_2=v^{(2)}+R\). with \(v_1\) having no radial Fourier mode. Differentiating the weighted equation at \(t=0\) gives \[ -\Delta v_1-j^2v_1=2j^2\operatorname{Re}(h)v_0 \] Here the first eigenvalue derivative is \[ \lambda'(0)=-2j^2\int_{\mathbb D}\operatorname{Re}(h)v_0^2dA=0, \] because \(v_0\) is radial and \(h\) has no constant coefficient; the derivative of the normalization contributes no radial mode either. Imposing \(v_1|_{\partial\mathbb D}=0\) gives the displayed Bessel solution \(w_n\); the Bessel recurrence gives \(w_n'(1)=-p_Dho_n/(n+1)\). Since \(X\hookrightarrow W^{1,4}(\mathbb D)\) for zero-boundary functions, the claimed \(W^{1,4}\) estimate follows. Set \(b_1=4\,
abla v_0\cdot
abla v_1\,|
abla v_0|^2\); angular orthogonality gives its zero circular mean. The pointwise inequality \[  igl||x+y|^4-|x|^4-4|x|^2x\cdot y igr|\le C(|x|^2|y|^2+|y|^4) \] with \(x=
abla v_0\) and \(y=t
abla v_1+
abla R_2\) gives the stated remainder after separately bounding the omitted linear term \(4|
abla v_0|^2
abla v_0\cdot
abla R_2\) by \(CS\) and using the \(X\) bounds for the quadratic terms. Because \(
abla v_0\) and \(
abla v_1\) are bounded and \(\|
abla R_2\|_{L^\infty}\le CS\), the same pointwise inequality gives the \(L^\infty\) remainder bound in the statement; the definition of \(b_1\) gives \(\|b_1\|_{L^\infty}\le C\). Finally angular orthogonality gives \[ 2\int_{\mathbb D}b_1(h)\operatorname{Re}k\,dA =\sum_{n\ge2}m_n\operatorname{Re}(h_n\overline{k_n}), \qquad m_n=8\pi\int_0^1v_0'(r)^3w_n'(r)r^{n+1}\,dr. \] Writing \(J_n(jr)/(r^nJ_n(j))\) as its Bessel power series, the denominator is at least \(1-j^2/[4(n+1)]>1/2\) for \(n\ge2\), and its derivative is \(O((n+1)^{-1})\). Together with \(w_n'(1)=O((n+1)^{-1})\) and \(A_0'(1)=0\) for \(A_0(r)=rv_0'(r)/p_D\), one obtains \(|w_n'(r)|\le Cr^{n-1}((1-r)^2+(1-r)/(n+1)+(n+1)^{-2})\). Integrating the three Beta functions gives \(|m_n|\le C(n+1)^{-3}\). Evaluating the expansion at the boundary also gives \[ p(	heta)=p_D+p_D\sum_{n\ge2} rac{ho_n}{n+1}\operatorname{Re}(g_ne^{in	heta})+r_p(	heta), \qquad \|r_p\|_{L^\infty}\le CS, \] and the same Bessel series gives \(|ho_n|\le C/(n+1)\).

By @def-conformal-data, \(g\) has no constant coefficient, so \(h\) has no constant coefficient when \(S>0\). Write \(g=th\), \(t=\sqrt S\), and \(\|h\|_{A^2}=1\). By @lem-c1-perturbation, \[ v=v_0+t v_1+e, \qquad \|e\|_{L^\infty(\mathbb D)}\le CS, \qquad \|v_1\|_{L^\infty(\mathbb D)}\le C, \] and \(v_1\) has no radial Fourier mode. By @lem-disk-perturbation, \(|\lambda-j^2|\le CS\). Since \(v_0\) is radial and \(h\) has no constant coefficient, angular orthogonality gives \[ \int_{\mathbb D}v_0^3v_1\,dA=0, \qquad \int_{\mathbb D}v_0^4\operatorname{Re}h\,dA=0. \] The boundedness of \(v_0,v_1,e\) and Cauchy–Schwarz imply \[ v^4=v_0^4+4t v_0^3v_1+E, \qquad \|E\|_{L^\infty(\mathbb D)}\le CS. \] Multiplying by \(|1+th|^2=1+2t\operatorname{Re}h+t^2|h|^2\) and using \(\|h\|_{L^1}\le C\|h\|_{A^2}\) gives \[ \left|\int_{\mathbb D}v^4|1+g|^2\,dA-\int_{\mathbb D}v_0^4\,dA\right|\le CS. \] Indeed the only terms of order \(t\) are the two displayed zero integrals; all remaining terms contain either \(E\), \(t^2|h|^2\), or the product \(t^2v_0^3v_1\operatorname{Re}h\) and are \(O(S)\). Therefore \[ \lambda^2\int_{\mathbb D}v^4|1+g|^2\,dA =j^4\int_{\mathbb D}v_0^4\,dA+O(S), \qquad \frac{\lambda^2}{\pi(1+S)}=\frac{j^4}{\pi}+O(S). \] The radial Bessel equation for \(v_0\), integrated by parts using \(v_0(1)=0\) and \(\int_{\mathbb D}v_0^2dA=1\), gives \[ \int_{\mathbb D}|\nabla v_0|^4\,dA =j^4\left(\int_{\mathbb D}v_0^4\,dA-\frac1\pi\right). \] Combining these displays proves the claim.

If \(S=0\) the assertion is immediate. Otherwise write \(g=th\) with \(t=\sqrt S\). By @def-conformal-data, \(k(0)=0\), so the constant coefficient of the analytic function \(k\) is zero and \[ \int_{\mathbb D}a\operatorname{Re}k\,dA=0 \] because \(a\) is radial. The function \(a\) is bounded below on the fixed annulus \(A_0=\{1/2\le|z|\le1\}\). The Bergman pointwise estimate on \(|z|\le1/2\) gives \(|g|\le C\sqrt S\) there, hence \(|k|\le C\sqrt S\) for small \(S\). Thus \[ T\le CS+C\int_{A_0}|k|^2\,dA \le CS+c^{-1}\int_{\mathbb D}a|k|^2\,dA. \] By @lem-gradient-perturbation, \(\|b_1\|_{L^\infty}\le C\) and, from the \(C^1\) remainder used in its proof, \(\|R_1\|_{L^\infty}\le CS\) for \(R_1=|\nabla v|^4-a-tb_1\). Expanding the weighted integral, using the vanishing radial pairing, and applying Cauchy–Schwarz gives \[ \begin{aligned} \int_{\mathbb D}|\nabla v|^4|1+k|^2\,dA &\ge \int_{\mathbb D}a\,dA+\int_{\mathbb D}a|k|^2\,dA\\ &\quad-C\bigl(\sqrt S\sqrt T+\sqrt S\,T+S+S\sqrt T+ST\bigr). \end{aligned} \] The first two errors come from \(t b_1(2\operatorname{Re}k+|k|^2)\), and the remaining ones from \(R_1(1+2\operatorname{Re}k+|k|^2)\). Since \(S\sqrt T\le S+ST\), the preceding control of \(T\) by the \(a|k|^2\) term yields the stated inequality after adjusting \(c,C\).

Under the edge-moment hypotheses @lem-edge-moments, @lem-airy-identity and the conformal change of variables in @def-conformal-data give \[ \int_{\mathbb D}|
abla v|^4|1+k|^2 =\lambda^2\int_{\mathbb D}v^4|1+g|^2- rac{\lambda^2}{\pi(1+S)}. \] By @lem-inverse-left-bound, the left-hand side is at least \[ \int_{\mathbb D}|
abla v_0|^4+cT-C\{S+\sqrt S\sqrt T+\sqrt S\,T+ST\}. \] By @lem-weighted-eigen-balance, the right-hand side is at most \[ \int_{\mathbb D}|
abla v_0|^4+CS. \] Comparing these bounds in the identity yields \[ T\le C\{S+\sqrt S\sqrt T+\sqrt S\,T+ST\}. \] Young’s inequality absorbs the mixed term and, for sufficiently small \(S\), the last two terms, proving \(T\le CS\).

Put \(D=g+k\). Since \(g+k=-gk\) by @def-conformal-data, Hölder gives \[ \|D\|_{A^1}\le \|g\|_{A^2}\|k\|_{A^2}\le CS, \qquad \|D\|_{A^2}^2\le2(S+T)\le CS. \] The constant and linear coefficients of \(D\) vanish. For every \(n\ge2\), the coefficient formula and the two bounds imply \[ |D_n|\le C(n+1)S, \qquad \sum_{n\ge2}\frac{|D_n|^2}{n+1}\le CS. \] With \(K=\lceil S^{-1/2}\rceil\), splitting at \(K\) gives \[ \sum_{n\ge2}\frac{|D_n|^2}{(n+1)^3} \le C S^2\sum_{n\le K}\frac1{n+1} +C(K+1)^{-2}\sum_{n>K}\frac{|D_n|^2}{n+1} \le CS^2\log(e/S). \] Let \(E=k-g\). Since \(|k_n|^2-|g_n|^2=\operatorname{Re}(D_n\overline{E_n})\), Cauchy–Schwarz gives \[ \left|\sum_{n\ge2}m_n(|k_n|^2-|g_n|^2)\right| \le C C_m \left(\sum_{n\ge2}\frac{|D_n|^2}{(n+1)^3}\right)^{1/2} \left(\sum_{n\ge2}\frac{|E_n|^2}{n+1}\right)^{1/2} \le C C_m S^{3/2}\sqrt{\log(e/S)}. \]Put \(W=L-g\). The scalar estimate \[ |e^z-1-z|\le C\bigl(|e^z-1|^2+|z|^2\bigr) \] and \(e^L-1=g\) give \(\|W\|_{A^1}\le CS\). Also \[ \|L\|_{A^2}^2\le(S+T)/2 \] because \(|e^L|^2+|e^{-L}|^2-2\ge4(\operatorname{Re}L)^2\) pointwise and the real and imaginary parts of an analytic function with zero constant term have equal Bergman energy. Hence \(\|W\|_{A^2}^2\le CS\). The same low/high frequency split gives \[ \sum_{n\ge2}\frac{|W_n|^2}{(n+1)^3}\le CS^2\log(e/S). \] Finally \(|L_n|^2-|g_n|^2=\operatorname{Re}(W_n\overline{(L_n+g_n)})\) and \(\sum|L_n+g_n|^2/(n+1)\le CS\), so the second estimate follows by Cauchy–Schwarz.

By @def-conformal-data, \(1+g\) is analytic and nonzero in \(\mathbb D\) with value \(1\) at the origin, so let \(L\) be the analytic logarithm normalized by \(L(0)=0\). Then \(1+g=e^L\) and \((1+g)^{-1}=1+k=e^{-L}\), and the pointwise identity \[ |1+g|^2+|1+k|^2-2 =2\cosh(2\operatorname{Re}L)-2 \ge4(\operatorname{Re}L)^2 \] holds. Integrating and using the definitions of \(S,T\) gives \[ S+T\ge4\|\operatorname{Re}L\|_{A^2}^2. \] The constant coefficient of \(L\) is zero because \((1+g)(0)=1\). For an analytic function with zero constant coefficient, Parseval gives equal Bergman energies for its real and imaginary parts, so \(\|L\|_{A^2}^2=2\|\operatorname{Re}L\|_{A^2}^2\). The displayed inequality follows.

By the diagonal representation in @lem-gradient-perturbation, with \(D=g+k\), \[ M(g,k)-M(g,-g)=M(g,D)=\sum_{n\ge2}m_n\operatorname{Re}(g_n\overline{D_n}), \qquad |m_n|\le C(n+1)^{-3}. \] The coefficient splitting in @lem-frequency-replacement gives \[ \sum_{n\ge2}\frac{|D_n|^2}{(n+1)^3}\le CS^2\log(e/S), \qquad \sum_{n\ge2}\frac{|g_n|^2}{n+1}=S. \] Cauchy–Schwarz with weights \((n+1)^{-3}\) and \((n+1)^{-1}\) proves the claim.

For one real monomial \(g=az^n\), the first-order disk equation in @lem-gradient-perturbation gives \[ v_1(r,\theta)=a w_n(r)\cos(n\theta), \qquad w_n(r)=\frac{r^{n+1}v_0'(r)+p_DJ_n(jr)/J_n(j)}{n+1}, \] and the Bessel recurrence gives \(w_n'(1)=-p_D\rho_n/(n+1)\). The physical flux is \(q=p^2/|1+g|^2\), so \[ \delta(q-c)=-\frac{2p_D^2\beta_n}{n+1}\operatorname{Re}(ae^{in\theta}). \] By @lem-airy-boundary-flux, the calibrated Airy boundary gradient satisfies \[ \frac{d\Gamma}{d\theta}=\frac12(q-c)i e^{i\theta}F'(e^{i\theta}). \] At the disk \(\Gamma\) is constant. Integrating the first variation gives frequencies \(n+1\) and \(1-n\). If \(d=-2p_D^2\beta_na/(n+1)\), the signed Fourier-area formula gives \[ \operatorname{Area}_{\rm signed}(\dot\Gamma)=-\frac{\pi d^2}{8(n^2-1)}. \] For the conformal pullback \(v=u\circ F\), the chain rule and \(dA_x=|F'|^2dA_z\) give \[ \int_\Omega|\nabla u|^4dA_x=\int_{\mathbb D}|\nabla v|^4|1+k|^2dA_z, \quad \int_\Omega u^4dA_x=\int_{\mathbb D}v^4|1+g|^2dA_z, \quad A(\Omega)=\pi(1+\|g\|_{A^2}^2). \] Thus the physical functional in @lem-airy-boundary-flux is the disk functional \(\mathscr H(g,k)\) on the inverse path \(k=(1+g)^{-1}-1\). The second identity of @lem-airy-boundary-flux therefore gives \(H_2=-4\) times this signed area, hence \[ H_2(az^n,-az^n)=2\pi p_D^4\frac{\beta_n^2}{(n+1)^2(n^2-1)}|a|^2. \] Rotation handles complex \(a\), and angular orthogonality eliminates mixed modes. Summing over finite polynomials proves the formula.

By @def-conformal-data, write \(F'=1+g\), \(k=(1+g)^{-1}-1\), \(S=\|g\|_{A^2}^2\), and \(T=\|k\|_{A^2}^2\). Let \(v(g)\) and \(\lambda(g)\) be the fixed-space positive branch from @lem-c1-perturbation and @lem-disk-perturbation. Treat \(g\) and \(k\) temporarily as independent analytic variables and define \[ \mathscr H(g,k)=\int_{\mathbb D}|
abla v(g)|^4|1+k|^2dA -\lambda(g)^2\int_{\mathbb D}v(g)^4|1+g|^2dA + rac{\lambda(g)^2}{\pi(1+\|g\|_{A^2}^2)}. \] The fixed-space expansion in @lem-c1-perturbation and the form expansion in @lem-disk-perturbation imply a uniform Taylor formula \[ \mathscr H(g,k)=H_2(g,k)+R_H(g,k), \qquad |R_H(g,k)|\le C(\|g\|_{A^2}+\|k\|_{A^2})^3. \] Here the constant and linear Taylor coefficients vanish. At \((g,k)=(0,0)\) the radial Bessel equation gives \[ \int_{\mathbb D}|
abla v_0|^4dA-j^4\int_{\mathbb D}v_0^4dA+ rac{j^4}{\pi}=0. \] For a first variation \(g=th\), the eigenvalue derivative is \(\lambda'(0)=0\) by angular orthogonality, the area term has zero derivative, and every term involving \(h\), \(v_1\), or \(k\) has zero angular mean because all these analytic perturbations have no constant coefficient. Thus \(D\mathscr H(0,0)=0\). Multiplying the second-order Taylor polynomials supplied by @lem-c1-perturbation (including its eigenvalue expansion) gives the displayed cubic remainder; products of two \(A^2\) factors are controlled by Cauchy–Schwarz and the \(C^1\) eigenfunction remainder is uniform.For the quadratic part, put \(a=|
abla v_0|^4\), \(p_D=j/\sqrt\pi\), and let \(b_1\) be the first gradient variation in @lem-gradient-perturbation. Direct multiplication gives \[ H_2(g,k)=\pi p_D^4(T-S)+Q_0(g)+A(k)+M(g,k), \] where \(A(k)=\int(a-p_D^4)|k|^2dA\) and \(M(g,k)=2\int b_1(g)\operatorname{Re}k\,dA\); \(Q_0\) contains the remaining pure quadratic terms in \(v(g)\), \(\lambda(g)\) and \(g\).For the quadratic part, the radial term \(A(k)\) has coefficients \(O((n+1)^{-2})\) by \(|a(r)-p_D^4|\le C(1-r)\). The phase-sensitive term is handled by @lem-bilinear-mode-replacement. The pure inverse-path quadratic form is exactly the Airy boundary calculation in @lem-airy-boundary-quadratic, and polynomial density extends it to all \(A^2\) data because its multiplier is \(O((n+1)^{-2})\). Thus \[ H_2(g,-g)=2\pi p_D^4\sum_{n\ge2}d_n|g_n|^2. \] For the actual inverse relation, @lem-frequency-replacement and @lem-bilinear-mode-replacement replace \(A(k)+M(g,k)\) by \(A(-g)+M(g,-g)\) with error \(O(S^{3/2}\sqrt{\log(e/S)})\). The same bound controls \(R_H\) because @lem-inverse-energy gives \(T\le CS\). Indeed, with \(v=u\circ F\), the chain rule and conformal Jacobian give \[ \int_P|
abla u|^4=\int_{\mathbb D}|
abla v|^4|1+k|^2dA, \quad \int_Pu^4=\int_{\mathbb D}v^4|1+g|^2dA, \quad A(P)=\pi(1+S), \] so @lem-airy-identity is exactly \(\mathscr H(g,k)=0\). Dividing by \(\pi p_D^4\) proves the formula.

The first-order perturbation and the second-order disk calculation from @lem-disk-perturbation give \[ \frac{J(P)}{\pi j^2}=1+S-\sum_{n\ge2}\frac{\rho_n}{(n+1)^2}|g_n|^2+O(S^{3/2}), \] with \(\beta_n=n+1-\rho_n\). By @lem-gradient-perturbation, @lem-inverse-energy and @lem-airy-quadratic-response, \[ S-T=2\sum_{n\ge2}\frac{\beta_n^2}{(n+1)^2(n^2-1)}|g_n|^2+O\bigl(S^{3/2}\sqrt{\log(e/S)}\bigr). \] By @lem-log-energy-bound, \(\|L\|_{A^2}^2\le(S+T)/2\), and by @lem-frequency-replacement every quadratic form with multiplier \(O((n+1)^{-2})\) may replace \(g\) by \(L\) at an error of order \(S^{3/2}\sqrt{\log(e/S)}\). Combining these facts with the scalar expansion gives Put \(d_n=\beta_n^2/((n+1)^2(n^2-1))\), \(r_n=\rho_n/(n+1)^2\), and \(E=S^{3/2}\sqrt{\log(e/S)}\). The Airy response gives \(T=S-2\sum d_n|g_n|^2+O(E)\), so the logarithmic bound gives \[ S\ge \|L\|_{A^2}^2+\sum_{n\ge2}d_n|g_n|^2-O(E). \] The scalar disk expansion therefore yields \[ \frac{J(P)}{\pi j^2} \ge1+\|L\|_{A^2}^2+\sum_{n\ge2}(d_n-r_n)|g_n|^2-O(E). \] Since \(0<\rho_n<2\) and \(0<\beta_n<n+1\), one has \[ |d_n-r_n|\le\frac{C}{(n+1)^2}. \] Thus @lem-frequency-replacement changes the last quadratic form from \(g\) to \(L\) at cost \(O(E)\). Since \(L(0)=L_1=0\), Bergman Parseval gives \(\|L\|_{A^2}^2=\sum_{n\ge2}|L_n|^2/(n+1)\), and \[ \frac1{n+1}+d_n-r_n =\frac{\beta_n}{(n+1)^2}\left(1+\frac{\beta_n}{n^2-1}\right). \] Finally, @def-turn-measure gives \(L_n=2\widehat\mu(n)/n\), so the coefficient becomes \(4a_n\) and the claimed inequality follows after shrinking \(S_0\) to absorb the \(O(S^{3/2})\) term into \(O(E)\). \[ \frac{J(P)}{\pi j^2}\ge1+\sum_{n\ge2}\frac{\beta_n}{(n+1)^2}\left(1+\frac{\beta_n}{n^2-1}\right)|L_n|^2-C S^{3/2}\sqrt{\log(e/S)}. \] Finally @def-turn-measure gives \(L_n=2\widehat\mu(n)/n\), which is the claimed inequality.

Define on \(\ell^2(\mathbb N_0)\) the self-adjoint matrix \[ A_{rs}=\tau^{(r+s)/2}\widehat\mu(r-s)=\sum_iw_i(v_i)_r\overline{(v_i)_s}, \qquad (v_i)_r=\tau^{r/2}e^{-ir\theta_i}. \] The Vandermonde vectors at distinct nodes are linearly independent, so \(A\) has exactly \(p\) positive eigenvalues \(\alpha_1\ge\cdots\ge\alpha_p>0\). The trace is \((1-\tau)^{-1}\), and the negative eigenvalues can only decrease the trace, hence \(Q:=\sum_i\alpha_i\ge(1-\tau)^{-1}\). The shift compression and the min–max principle give \(\alpha_{i+1}\le\tau\alpha_i\). For fixed \(Q\) and these ratio constraints, a finite exchange argument (move mass from an earlier coordinate to the latest coordinate until the active constraint is met) shows that the minimum of the strictly convex function \(\sum_i\alpha_i^2\) is attained at \[ \alpha_i=Q\frac{(1-\tau)\tau^{i-1}}{1-\tau^p},\qquad 1\le i\le p. \] Consequently \[ \sum_i\alpha_i^2\ge Q^2\frac{1-\tau}{1+\tau}\frac{1+\tau^p}{1-\tau^p} \ge\frac{1+\tau^p}{(1-\tau^2)(1-\tau^p)}. \] On the other hand, \[ \|A\|_{HS}^2=\frac{1+2\sum_{n\ge1}\tau^n|\widehat\mu(n)|^2}{1-\tau^2} \] and the Hilbert–Schmidt norm dominates the squared positive eigenvalues. Rearranging gives \[ 1+2\sum_{n\ge1}\tau^n|\widehat\mu(n)|^2\ge\frac{1+\tau^p}{1-\tau^p}, \] which is exactly the claimed bound.

By @lem-spectral-core and @def-positive-kernel, the coefficients \(a_n\), \(b_n\), \(\rho_n\), \(\kappa\), and the energy \(E_b\) have the stated meanings. The Bessel bounds \(5.78<j^2<5.8\) give \(1.89<\kappa<1.9\). The recurrence for \(J_n\) implies \(0<\rho_n<2\) and, for \(n\ge3\), \(\rho_n<n\alpha/(n^2+\kappa)\) with \(\alpha=\kappa+1\). Substitution into \[ a_n=\frac{n-\rho_n+\rho_n^2/(n+1)^2}{n^2(n^2-1)} \] proves \(a_n\ge b_n\); for \(n=2\), the identity \(J_0(j)=0\) reduces the inequality to \(\kappa^3+7\kappa^2+12\kappa-54\ge0\), which holds for \(\kappa\ge1.89\).The Laplace representation follows from \[ \int_0^\infty e^{-nt}(1-\cos(\sqrt\kappa t))\,dt=\frac{\kappa}{n(n^2+\kappa)}. \] Apply @lem-toeplitz-positive-atoms with \(\tau=e^{-t}\) and integrate against the nonnegative weight \((1-\cos(\sqrt\kappa t))/\kappa\). Tonelli’s theorem gives \(E_b(\mu)\ge B_p\).

By @lem-spectral-core and @lem-kernel-comparison, \(a_n\ge b_n\) for \(n\ge2\). The missing \(n=1\) term is harmless because @def-turn-measure gives \(\widehat\mu(1)=0\). Hence \[ \frac{J(P)}{\pi j^2}\ge 1+4E_b(\mu)-C S^{3/2}\sqrt{\log(e/S)}. \] The lower bound \(E_b(\mu)\ge B_p\) is exactly @lem-kernel-comparison.

By @def-positive-kernel, \(p\ge1\), \(\kappa>0\), and \[ B_p=\sum_{\ell\ge1}\frac1{\ell p((\ell p)^2+\kappa)}. \] For each \(\ell\ge1\), \[ \frac1{\ell p((\ell p)^2+\kappa)} =\frac1{\ell^3p^3}-\frac{\kappa}{\ell^5p^5}+O\left(\frac{1}{\ell^7p^7}\right), \] uniformly for large \(p\), by the geometric expansion of \((1+\kappa/(\ell p)^2)^{-1}\). Summing the absolutely convergent remainders gives the stated asymptotic. Each summand decreases strictly with \(p\), so \(B_p\) is decreasing.

Write \[ J_n(j)=\frac{(j/2)^n}{n!}H_n, \qquad H_n=\sum_{m\ge0}\frac{(-j^2/4)^m n!}{m!(n+m)!}. \] The alternating-series estimate gives \(H_n\ge1-j^2/[4(n+1)]>1/2\) for \(n\ge2\), while absolute summation gives \(|H_{n+1}|\le C\). Hence \[ \rho_n=\frac{j^2}{2(n+1)}\frac{H_{n+1}}{H_n}, \] which proves the upper bound. Positivity follows from the standard interlacing of the first positive zeros, since \(j_{0,1}<j_{n,1}\) and \(J_n(j)>0\) for \(n\ge1\).

By @def-conformal-data, \(r_{R_M}\) denotes the conformal-radius function used in the normalization. We use the standard theorem that the conformal-radius function of a bounded convex planar domain is concave. The regular polygon is convex and invariant under the rotations \(\sigma_k(z)=e^{2\pi ik/M}z\). For every \(z\) in the polygon, \[ 0=\frac1M\sum_{k=0}^{M-1}\sigma_k(z). \] Concavity and rotational invariance give \[ r_{R_M}(0)\ge\frac1M\sum_{k=0}^{M-1}r_{R_M}(\sigma_kz)=r_{R_M}(z). \] Thus the center is a maximizer. Uniqueness of the centered Riemann map after fixing \(F_M'(0)>0\) and equivariance under the rotation group imply \(F_M(e^{2\pi i/M}z)=e^{2\pi i/M}F_M(z)\); differentiating twice at \(0\) gives \(F_M''(0)=0\).

Write \[ c_q=\frac\alpha qP_q, \qquad P_q=\prod_{r=1}^{q-1}\left(1+\frac\alpha r\right), \qquad H_q=\sum_{r=1}^q\frac1r. \] Set \(Q=\lfloor e^{1/(4\alpha)}\rfloor\). For \(q\le Q\), \(\alpha H_{q-1}\le1/2\) and the product expansion with a positive remainder gives \[ P_q=1+\alpha H_{q-1}+R_q, \qquad |R_q|\le C\alpha^2(1+H_{q-1}^2). \] Also \[ \frac1{qM+1}=\frac1{qM}-\frac1{q^2M^2}+O\left(\frac1{q^3M^3}\right). \] Substitution, using convergence of \(\sum q^{-3}\), \(\sum H_{q-1}q^{-3}\) and \(\sum(1+H_{q-1}^2)q^{-3}\), gives \[ \sum_{q\le Q}\frac{c_q^2}{qM+1} =\frac{\alpha^2}{M}\zeta(3) +\frac{2\alpha^3}{M}\sum_{q\ge1}\frac{H_{q-1}}{q^3} -\frac{\alpha^2}{M^2}\zeta(4)+O(M^{-5}). \] The standard Euler sum \(\sum_{q\ge1}H_{q-1}/q^3=\zeta(4)/4\) and \(\alpha=2/M\) make the two \(M^{-4}\) terms cancel, leaving \(4\zeta(3)M^{-3}+O(M^{-5})\).For \(q>Q\), the Gamma-ratio estimate \(P_q\le Cq^\alpha\) gives \[ \sum_{q>Q}\frac{c_q^2}{qM+1} \le\frac{C\alpha^2}{M}\sum_{q>Q}q^{-3+2\alpha} \le C M^{-3}e^{-1/(2\alpha)}=O(M^{-5}). \] This proves the claim.

By @lem-regular-center-maximizer, the centered map below is the normalized map required by @def-conformal-data. The regular \(M\)-gon is invariant under rotations about its center, and its Schwarz–Christoffel derivative is \[ F_M'(z)=(1-z^M)^{-2/M}=1+g_M(z),qquad g_M(z)=\sum_{q\ge1}c_qz^{qM},qquad c_q=\frac{(2/M)_q}{q!}. \] By @lem-regular-sc-coefficient-sum and @def-conformal-data, \[ S_M=\sum_{q\ge1}\frac{c_q^2}{qM+1} =\frac{4\zeta(3)}{M^3}+O(M^{-5}). \]Apply @lem-disk-perturbation to \(g_M\). The quadratic correction satisfies \[ \left|\sum_{q\ge1}\frac{\rho_{qM}}{(qM+1)^2}c_q^2\right| \le \frac{C}{M^2}\sum_{q\ge1}\frac{c_q^2}{qM+1}=O(M^{-5}), \] using @lem-bessel-ratio-decay. Since \(S_M=O(M^{-3})\), it is below the fixed perturbation threshold for all sufficiently large \(M\), and \(S_M^{3/2}=O(M^{-9/2})\). The perturbation expansion yields \[ \frac{J(R_M)}{\pi j^2}=1+\frac{4\zeta(3)}{M^3}+O(M^{-9/2}). \]

Assume for contradiction that there is a sequence of such polygons with \(N\to\infty\) and \(J(P)\le J(R_{N-1})\). If there are at least two reflex corners, the number \(p\) of convex corners is at most \(N-2\). By @lem-near-circle-conformal, \(S\le CN^{-3}\), and @lem-signed-turn-lower-bound gives \[ \frac{J(P)}{\pi j^2}\ge1+4B_p-C S^{3/2}\sqrt{\log(e/S)}. \] By @lem-bp-asymptotic, \(B_p\ge B_{N-2}\) and \[ B_{N-2}=\zeta(3)(N-2)^{-3}+O(N^{-5}). \] The conformal estimate makes the error \(o(N^{-4})\). By @lem-regular-polygon-asymptotic, \[ 4B_{N-2}-\frac{4\zeta(3)}{(N-1)^3}=12\zeta(3)N^{-4}+O(N^{-5})>0 \] for large \(N\), so the lower bound is strictly larger than \(J(R_{N-1})/(\pi j^2)\), contradicting the assumed upper bound.

By @def-conformal-data, put \(H(z)=F(z)-F(0)-z\). The homogeneous boundary \(H^{1/2}\) seminorm satisfies \[ \int_0^{2\pi}\!\int_0^{2\pi}  rac{|H(e^{i	heta})-H(e^{i\varphi})|^2}{|e^{i	heta}-e^{i\varphi}|^2},d	heta d\varphi =4\pi^2S. \] On a straight edge, a fixed unit normal \(
u\) makes \(
u\cdot F(e^{i	heta})\) constant. Restricting the double integral to the edge arc and projecting onto \(
u\) gives the quotient of the difference of \(
u\cdot e^{i	heta}\) by \(e^{i	heta}-e^{i\varphi}\). After centering the arc, the sine part contributes \(c\varepsilon^2\) and the cosine part contributes \(c\varepsilon^4\); the mixed term vanishes by \((	heta,\varphi)\mapsto(-	heta,-\varphi)\). Thus the restricted integral is at least \(c\varepsilon^4\), proving the claim.

By @lem-gradient-perturbation, write \(g=th\) and use the boundary expansion \[ p(\theta)=p_D+p_D\sum_{n\ge2}\frac{\rho_n}{n+1}\operatorname{Re}(g_ne^{in\theta})+O(S) \] uniformly. The pointwise sum is \(O(\sqrt S)\) by Cauchy–Schwarz. For \(|t|\le\varepsilon\le1\), \[ |p(\theta+t)-p(\theta)| \le C\sqrt S\left(\sum_{n\ge2}\frac{\min(n^2t^2,4)}{(n+1)^3}\right)^{1/2}+CS \le C\sqrt S\,\varepsilon\sqrt{\log(e/\varepsilon)}+CS. \] By @lem-prevertex-gap, \(\varepsilon\le CS^{1/4}\), and the displayed bound follows after enlarging the constant. The same pointwise estimate gives \(\|p-p_D\|_\infty\le C\sqrt S+CS\); choosing \(S\) small gives both \(p\ge p_D/2\) and \(p\le2p_D\).

By @def-turn-measure, the normalized map has prevertices \(0=\theta_0<\theta_1<\cdots<\theta_p<2\pi\), weights \(-b\) at \(0\) and \(a_j>0\) at the other prevertices, and \[ \log F'(z)=\mathrm{const}+2b\log(1-z)-2\sum_j a_j\log(1-e^{-i\theta_j}z). \] On the boundary, write \(x=\cot(\theta/2)\) and \(x_j=\cot(\theta_j/2)\). Differentiating the real part of this formula gives \[ (\log h)'=bx+C_*+\sum_j\frac{a_j(1+x_j^2)}{x-x_j}, \qquad C_*:=\sum_ja_jx_j. \] If \(C_*\ge0\), choose the first edge to the right of \(0\); its parameter interval lies in \((0,\theta_1)\), so \(x>0\) and \(x>x_j\) for every positive prevertex. If \(C_*<0\), choose the last edge to the left; its interval lies in \((\theta_p,2\pi)\), so \(x<0\) and \(x<x_j\) for every positive prevertex. Thus all terms have one sign. Reverse orientation if needed so \(h\) decreases. If the selected edge has parameter length \(\varepsilon\), its positive endpoint has weight \(a\). On its central subarc \([\varepsilon/4,3\varepsilon/4]\), the endpoint term is \[ \frac{1+\cot^2(\varepsilon/2)}{\cot(\theta/2)-\cot(\varepsilon/2)} =\frac{\sin(\theta/2)}{\sin(\varepsilon/2)\sin((\varepsilon-\theta)/2)}\ge c/\varepsilon. \] The negative atom contributes the same lower bound with \(b\); integrating over the central half gives the stated logarithmic drop.

By @def-admissible-polygon, @def-stationary-polygon, and @def-conformal-data, \(E\) is an effective edge and \(v=u\circ F\), \(h=|F'|\). The conformal chain rule gives \(|\nabla u(F(z))|=|\nabla v(z)|/|F'(z)|\) on the relative interior of \(E\); since both functions vanish there, their gradients are normal, hence \(q=p^2/h^2\). If \(L_E=\int h(\theta)d\theta\) and \(x=L_E^{-1}\int_0^\theta h(s)ds\), then \(dx=h(\theta)d\theta/L_E\) and the two edge moments in @lem-edge-moments become \[ \int_0^1(q-c)dx=0, \qquad \int_0^1x(q-c)dx=0. \] Subtracting one half of the first equation from the second gives the displayed centered identity.

After reversing the interval assume \(h\) decreases. Put \(H=\int_0^\varepsilon h(s)ds\) and use the coordinate \(x(s)\) and transformed weight \(\widetilde k_0\) from the statement. A direct change of variables in the two ordered double integrals gives \[ \int_{s<t}\frac{h(s)}{h(t)}dsdt=H^2\int_0^1x\widetilde k_0(x)dx, \qquad \int_{s<t}\left(\frac{h(s)}{h(t)}+\frac{h(t)}{h(s)}\right)dsdt=H^2\int_0^1\widetilde k_0(x)dx. \] Consequently, \[ D=\frac{2\int_0^1(x-1/2)\widetilde k_0(x)dx}{\int_0^1\widetilde k_0(x)dx}. \] Let \(m=\min_{[0,1]}p(s(x))^2\). The centered condition gives \[ \left|\int_0^1(x-1/2)\widetilde k_0dx\right| =\frac1m\left|\int_0^1(x-1/2)(m-p(s(x))^2)\widetilde k_0dx\right| \le \frac{\operatorname{osc}(p^2)}{2m}\int_0^1\widetilde k_0dx. \] Since \(m\ge p_0^2\) and \(p\le C_0p_0\), \(\operatorname{osc}(p^2)\le(C_0+1)p_0\operatorname{osc}p\), and the identity gives the claimed bound with a constant depending only on \(C_0\).

Here \(p_D=j/\sqrt\pi>0\) is fixed, so the factor \(1/p_D\) below is universal. By @lem-reflex-monotone-edge, the selected adjacent edge has monotone \(h\) and a central logarithmic drop at least \(c(a+v)\). On the two central rectangles, the ratio \(h(s)/h(t)\) is at least \(e^{c(a+v)}\), while the denominator is positive; hence the elementary rectangle comparison gives \[ D_I\ge c\min\{a+v,1\}. \] By @lem-physical-pressure-moment, the edge moments give the centered condition in the normalized physical coordinate, and @lem-monotone-weight-comparison applies with \(p_0=p_D/2\), \(C_0=4\) once \(S\) is sufficiently small. By @lem-edge-pressure-oscillation, \(p_D/2\le p\le2p_D\) and therefore \[ D_I\le C\operatorname{osc}_I p/p_D\le C'\operatorname{osc}_I p. \] The right-hand side is \(O(S^{3/4}\sqrt{\log(e/S)})\), so after decreasing the universal small-\(S\) threshold it is below the fixed constant in the lower bound whenever \(a+v\ge1\). Thus \(a+v<1\), and the lower bound becomes \(D_I\ge c(a+v)\). Combining the inequalities proves the result.

By @def-admissible-polygon, the unique reflex weight satisfies \(0<v<1/2\). The hypotheses of @lem-near-circle-conformal and @lem-disk-perturbation are met, so \(S\le CN^{-3}\) and the pressure estimate applies. By @lem-prevertex-gap and @lem-edge-pressure-oscillation, every edge arc has length at most \(CS^{1/4}\) and \[ \operatorname{osc}_I p\le CS^{3/4}\sqrt{\log(e/S)}. \] The one-reflex comparison @lem-reflex-edge-pressure-comparison gives, for one adjacent positive atom \(a\) and the negative mass \(v\), \[ c(a+v)\le D_I\le C\operatorname{osc}_I p. \] Thus \(a\le C S^{3/4}\sqrt{\log(e/S)}\). results.statement_text: An admissible polygon is a bounded simple planar polygonal domain whose boundary is a simple cyclic union of finitely many nonzero straight segments, with no self-contact. A genuine corner is a boundary vertex at which the two incident directed segments are not collinear; its interior angle is required to lie strictly between \(0\) and \(2\pi\). Starting from any polygonal presentation, delete adjacent collinear redundant vertices cyclically until no such vertex remains; the resulting effective-edge count is the invariant number \(N\), and \(A(P)\) is the Euclidean area. The cyclic deletion is independent of deletion order because it removes exactly the vertices at which the incoming and outgoing segment directions agree.

By @def-conformal-data, \(g\) is analytic, has no constant or linear coefficient, and satisfies \(S=\|g\|_{A^2}^2\); its normalized conformal pullback is the weighted disk problem used below. Put \(d(z)=1-|z|\). The Green kernel of the disk satisfies \[ |
abla_xG_D(x,z)|\le C|x-z|^{-1}, \qquad |
abla_xG_D(x,z)|\le C rac{d(z)}{|x-z|^2}. \] The Bergman pointwise estimate gives \(|g(z)|\le C\|g\|_{A^2}/d(z)\) for \(g\in A^2\) with vanishing constant coefficient. If \(h\in X\), then \(|h(z)|\le d(z)\|h\|_X\). Splitting the Green integral into \(|x-z|<d(x)/2\), the annulus \(d(x)/2\le|x-z|<2d(x)\), and dyadic outer annuli, the two kernel bounds give \[ \|G_D(gh)\|_X\le C\|g\|_{A^2}\|h\|_X, \qquad \|G_D(g_1\overline{g_2}h)\|_X\le C\|g_1\|_{A^2}\|g_2\|_{A^2}\|h\|_X. \] For example, in the near region \(d(z)\simeq d(x)\) and the pointwise bounds leave an integrable \(|x-z|^{-1}\) kernel; in the outer annuli \(d(z)\le d(x)+|x-z|\) cancels one power of the second Green bound, and Cauchy–Schwarz gives \(\|g_1g_2\|_{L^1}\le C\|g_1\|_{A^2}\|g_2\|_{A^2}\). Polynomial approximation extends these estimates to all \(A^2\) data, and the Green potential has a continuous boundary derivative.Define the real quadratic compact-operator family \[ K_g h=G_D[|1+g|^2h]=G_D[h+2\operatorname{Re}(g)h+|g|^2h] \] onlinearly in \(g\). The estimates give \(\|K_g-K_0\|_{B(X)}\le C(\sqrt S+S)\). The operator \(K_0\) is compact on \(X\) by disk Poisson regularity and the compact embedding \(C^{2,\alpha}(\overline{\mathbb D})\Subset C^1(\overline{\mathbb D})\). Its nonzero eigenvalues are the reciprocals of the Dirichlet eigenvalues; \(1/j^2\) is an isolated simple eigenvalue.Choose a fixed small contour \(\Gamma\) enclosing only \(1/j^2\). For \(S\) small, the Neumann series uniformly bounds \((zI-K_g)^{-1}\) on \(\Gamma\) and defines the rank-one Riesz projection \[ \Pi_g= rac1{2\pi i}\int_\Gamma(zI-K_g)^{-1}\,dz. \] The normalized vector \[ \widetilde v(g)=\Pi_gv_0, \qquad v(g)= rac{\widetilde v(g)}{\left(\int_{\mathbb D}\widetilde v(g)^2|1+g|^2ight)^{1/2}} \] therefore depends real-analytically on \(g\) in a fixed \(A^2\) neighborhood; the denominator stays uniformly away from zero. Writing \(g=t h\), define \(v_1=Dv(0)[h]\). Differentiating \[ -\Delta v=\lambda|1+th|^2v, \qquad \int_{\mathbb D}v^2|1+th|^2dA=1 \] at \(t=0\) gives \[ (-\Delta-j^2)v_1=2j^2\operatorname{Re}(h)v_0+\lambda'(0)v_0, \qquad \lambda'(0)=-2j^2\int_{\mathbb D}\operatorname{Re}(h)v_0^2dA=0. \] The last equality uses that \(v_0\) is radial and \(h\) has no constant coefficient. Separating variables and imposing the zero boundary value yields \[ v_1(r,	heta)=\sum_{n\ge2}w_n(r)\operatorname{Re}(h_ne^{in	heta}), \qquad w_n(r)= rac{r^{n+1}v_0'(r)+p_DJ_n(jr)/J_n(j)}{n+1}. \] The Bessel recurrence gives \(w_n'(1)=-p_Dho_n/(n+1)\). abla\phi|^2\,dA, \qquad \phi\in H^1_0(\mathbb D), \] which follows from Hardy’s inequality, shows that the pulled-back eigenfunction belongs to the weighted Dirichlet space. The positive solution is the principal branch by the variational characterization of the weighted Dirichlet eigenvalue. Since \(v_0(r)\ge c(1-r)\) and \(\|v-v_0\|_X\le C\sqrt S\), the branch is strictly positive in \(\mathbb D\). This proves the lemma.
results.statement_text: Let \[ X=\{\phi\in C^1(\overline{\mathbb D};\mathbb R):\phi|_{\partial\mathbb D}=0\}, \qquad \|\phi\|_X=\|\nabla\phi\|_{L^\infty}. \] For normalized conformal data from @def-conformal-data with \(S=\|g\|_{A^2}^2\) sufficiently small, writing \(g=t h\) with \(t=\sqrt S\) and \(\|h\|_{A^2}=1\), the pulled-back first eigenfunction has a uniform real-analytic expansion \[ v=v_0+t v_1+v^{(2)}+R, \qquad \|v_1\|_X\le C, \qquad \|v^{(2)}\|_X\le CS, \qquad \|R\|_X\le CS^{3/2}, \] where \(v_0(r)=J_0(jr)/(\sqrt\pi J_1(j))\), \(v_1\) has no radial Fourier mode, and the corresponding eigenvalue branch is the positive first branch. More precisely, with \(g=th\), \[ (-\Delta-j^2)v_1=2j^2\operatorname{Re}(h)v_0\quad\text{in }\mathbb D, \qquad v_1|_{\partial\mathbb D}=0. \] If \(h(z)=\sum_{n\ge2}h_nz^n\), then \[ v_1(r,\theta)=\sum_{n\ge2}w_n(r)\operatorname{Re}(h_ne^{in\theta}), \quad w_n(r)=\frac{r^{n+1}v_0'(r)+p_DJ_n(jr)/J_n(j)}{n+1}, \] where \(p_D=j/\sqrt\pi\) and \(w_n'(1)=-p_D\rho_n/(n+1)\) with \(\rho_n=jJ_{n+1}(j)/J_n(j)\). The same branch has a real-analytic eigenvalue expansion \[ \lambda(g)=j^2+\lambda^{(1)}(g)+\lambda^{(2)}(g)+O(\|g\|_{A^2}^3), \] where \(\lambda^{(r)}\) is homogeneous of degree \(r\).

For \(g\in A^2\) with no constant or linear term, the Bergman pointwise estimate gives \(|g(z)|\le C\|g\|_{A^2}/d(z)\). Consequently, Hardy’s inequality gives, for all \(\varphi,\psi\in H^1_0(\mathbb D)\), \[ \left|\int_{\mathbb D}2\operatorname{Re}(g)\varphi\psiight|\le C\sqrt S\,\|\varphi\|_{H^1_0}\|\psi\|_{H^1_0},\qquad \left|\int_{\mathbb D}|g|^2\varphi\psiight|\le CS\,\|\varphi\|_{H^1_0}\|\psi\|_{H^1_0}. \] Indeed \(|g|^2\le CS/d^2\), \(\int|\varphi|^2/d^2\le4\int|

The simple disk eigenvalue is isolated by a fixed spectral gap. The form version of analytic simple-eigenvalue perturbation therefore gives, uniformly in such \(h\), \[ v=v_0+t v_1+t^2v_2+O_{H^1_0}(t^3), \qquad \lambda= j^2+t\lambda_1+t^2\lambda_2+O(t^3). \] The case \(S=0\) is the disk and the assertion is immediate, so assume \(S>0\). The first variation is \(\lambda_1=-j^2\int_{\mathbb D}(h+ ar h)v_0^2=0\) because \(v_0\) is radial and \(h\) has no constant coefficient. Write \(v_0(r)=J_0(jr)/(\sqrt\pi J_1(j))\) and \(p_D=j/\sqrt\pi\). For the real mode \(h=a z^n\), the first-order equation in the \(n\)th angular sector has the explicit solution \[ v_1(r,	heta)=a w_n(r)\cos(n	heta),\qquad w_n(r)= rac{r^{n+1}v_0'(r)+p_DJ_n(jr)/J_n(j)}{n+1}. \] The Bessel equation verifies the radial equation and \(w_n(1)=0\). The second-order solvability condition is \[  rac{\lambda_2}{j^2a^2}=-2\pi\int_0^1\left(r^{2n+1}v_0(r)^2+r^{n+1}v_0(r)w_n(r)ight)dr. \] Substitution of \(w_n\) and one integration by parts reduce this to \[  rac{\lambda_2}{j^2a^2}=- rac{ho_n}{(n+1)^2}, \qquad ho_n=j rac{J_{n+1}(j)}{J_n(j)},\qquad 0<ho_n<2. \] The only nontrivial radial integral is \[ \int_0^1r^{n+1}v_0(r)J_n(jr)\,dr = rac{J_{n+1}(j)}{2\sqrt\pi(n+1)}, \] which follows by one integration by parts from the Bessel equation. Since \(A(P)=\pi(1+S)\) in @def-conformal-data, this yields the uniform expansion \[  rac{J(P)}{\pi j^2}=1+S-\sum_{n\ge2} rac{ho_n}{(n+1)^2}|g_n|^2+O(S^{3/2}). \] The perturbed branch remains the first eigenvalue by the weighted min–max principle: the mass form \(\int|1+g|^2|\varphi|^2\) is positive on nonzero \(H^1_0\) functions, and the branch is the positive continuation of the disk ground state. The sine mode is obtained by a phase rotation, and polarization plus density of analytic polynomials extends the second-order form from real monomials to arbitrary complex \(h\in A^2\). e0\) and \(0<ho_n<2\) hold for the first zero \(j=j_{0,1}\). Thus \[  rac{\lambda}{j^2}=1-\sum_{n\ge2} rac{ho_n}{(n+1)^2}|g_n|^2+O(S^{3/2}). \] Multiplying by \(A(P)/(\pi)=1+S\) from @def-conformal-data produces the displayed \(J\) expansion; the cross term \(S\sumho_n|g_n|^2/(n+1)^2\) is \(O(S^2)\) and is absorbed in \(O(S^{3/2})\). Since \(0<ho_n<2\) and \(n+1\ge3\), \[ \sum_{n\ge2} rac{ho_n}{(n+1)^2}|g_n|^2 \le2\sum_{n\ge2} rac{|g_n|^2}{(n+1)^2} \le rac23\sum_{n\ge2} rac{|g_n|^2}{n+1}= rac23S. \] Therefore the quadratic part of the full expression is at least \(S/3\); after shrinking the universal small neighborhood so that the \(CS^{3/2}\) remainder is at most \(S/6\), \(J(P)/(\pi j^2)-1\ge S/6\). results.statement_text: There are universal constants \(S_0,C>0\) such that, for normalized conformal data from @def-conformal-data with \(S\le S_0\), if \(v\) is the positive first solution of \[ -\Delta v=\lambda|1+g|^2v\quad\text{in }\mathbb D,qquad v|_{\partial\mathbb D}=0,qquad \int_{\mathbb D}v^2|1+g|^2=1, \] then, with \(J\) as in @def-j-functional, \[ \frac{J(P)}{\pi j^2}=1+S-\sum_{n\ge2}\frac{\rho_n}{(n+1)^2}|g_n|^2+R(g),qquad |R(g)|\le CS^{3/2}, \] where \(j=j_{0,1}\) is the first positive zero of \(J_0\), \(\rho_n=jJ_{n+1}(j)/J_n(j)\), and \(0<\rho_n<2\). In particular, \[ \frac{J(P)}{\pi j^2}-1\ge S/6. \] Moreover, writing \(g=t h\) with \(t=\sqrt S\) and \(\|h\|_{A^2}=1\), the corresponding normalized eigenpair satisfies \[ \|v-v_0\|_{H^1_0(\mathbb D)}\le Ct, \qquad |\lambda-j^2|\le Ct^2. \]

results.proof_text: By @def-stationary-polygon, the derivative of \(J=A\lambda\) vanishes for every vertex displacement. Hadamard’s formula is \[ DJ[V]=A\int_{\partial P}(c-q)V\cdot\nu\,ds. \] Moving one endpoint of an effective edge while keeping the other fixed produces an affine normal velocity on that edge, and the two endpoint velocities give the independent functions \(1\) and \(s/\ell_E\). Since adjacent effective edge normals are linearly independent at a genuine corner, stationarity forces both coefficients of these two affine test functions to vanish. Rescaling \(s/\ell_E\) gives the displayed moments.
results.statement_text: Let \(P\) be admissible and stationary in the sense of @def-stationary-polygon. If \(u>0\) is the \(L^2\)-normalized first eigenfunction, \(\lambda=\lambda_1(P)\), \(c=\lambda/A(P)\), and \(q=|\partial_\nu u|^2\), then every effective edge \(E\), parametrized by physical arclength \(s\in[0,\ell_E]\), satisfies \[ \int_E(q-c)\,ds=0,\qquad \int_Es(q-c)\,ds=0. \]

results.proof_text: Put \(D=g+k\). Since \(g+k=-gk\) by @def-conformal-data, Hölder gives \[ \|D\|_{A^1}\le \|g\|_{A^2}\|k\|_{A^2}\le CS, \qquad \|D\|_{A^2}^2\le2(S+T)\le CS. \] The constant and linear coefficients of \(D\) vanish. For every \(n\ge2\), the coefficient formula and the two bounds imply \[ |D_n|\le C(n+1)S, \qquad \sum_{n\ge2}\frac{|D_n|^2}{n+1}\le CS. \] With \(K=\lceil S^{-1/2}\rceil\), splitting at \(K\) gives \[ \sum_{n\ge2}\frac{|D_n|^2}{(n+1)^3} \le C S^2\sum_{n\le K}\frac1{n+1} +C(K+1)^{-2}\sum_{n>K}\frac{|D_n|^2}{n+1} \le CS^2\log(e/S). \] Let \(E=k-g\). Since \(|k_n|^2-|g_n|^2=\operatorname{Re}(D_n\overline{E_n})\), Cauchy–Schwarz gives \[ \left|\sum_{n\ge2}m_n(|k_n|^2-|g_n|^2)\right| \le C C_m \left(\sum_{n\ge2}\frac{|D_n|^2}{(n+1)^3}\right)^{1/2} \left(\sum_{n\ge2}\frac{|E_n|^2}{n+1}\right)^{1/2} \le C C_m S^{3/2}\sqrt{\log(e/S)}. \]Put \(W=L-g\). The scalar estimate \[ |e^z-1-z|\le C\bigl(|e^z-1|^2+|z|^2\bigr) \] and \(e^L-1=g\) give \(\|W\|_{A^1}\le CS\). Also \[ \|L\|_{A^2}^2\le(S+T)/2 \] because \(|e^L|^2+|e^{-L}|^2-2\ge4(\operatorname{Re}L)^2\) pointwise and the real and imaginary parts of an analytic function with zero constant term have equal Bergman energy. Hence \(\|W\|_{A^2}^2\le CS\). The same low/high frequency split gives \[ \sum_{n\ge2}\frac{|W_n|^2}{(n+1)^3}\le CS^2\log(e/S). \] Finally \(|L_n|^2-|g_n|^2=\operatorname{Re}(W_n\overline{(L_n+g_n)})\) and \(\sum|L_n+g_n|^2/(n+1)\le CS\), so the second estimate follows by Cauchy–Schwarz.
results.statement_text: Let \(g,k,L\) be the normalized analytic data in @def-conformal-data, with \(L=\log(1+g)\), and suppose \(S=\|g\|_{A^2}^2\) is sufficiently small and \(T\le CS\). If \((m_n)_{n\ge2}\) is any real sequence with \(|m_n|\le C_m(n+1)^{-2}\), then \[ \left|\sum_{n\ge2}m_n\bigl(|k_n|^2-|g_n|^2\bigr)\right| \le C C_m S^{3/2}\sqrt{\log(e/S)}, \] and \[ \left|\sum_{n\ge2}m_n\bigl(|L_n|^2-|g_n|^2\bigr)\right| \le C C_m S^{3/2}\sqrt{\log(e/S)}. \] In addition, for \(D=g+k\), \[ \sum_{n\ge2}\frac{|D_n|^2}{(n+1)^3} \le CS^2\log(e/S). \] The constant is independent of the polygonal angles and vertex separation.

results.proof_text: If \(S=0\) the assertion is immediate. Otherwise write \(g=th\) with \(t=\sqrt S\). By @def-conformal-data, \(k(0)=0\), so the constant coefficient of the analytic function \(k\) is zero and \[ \int_{\mathbb D}a\operatorname{Re}k\,dA=0 \] because \(a\) is radial. The function \(a\) is bounded below on the fixed annulus \(A_0=\{1/2\le|z|\le1\}\). The Bergman pointwise estimate on \(|z|\le1/2\) gives \(|g|\le C\sqrt S\) there, hence \(|k|\le C\sqrt S\) for small \(S\). Thus \[ T\le CS+C\int_{A_0}|k|^2\,dA \le CS+c^{-1}\int_{\mathbb D}a|k|^2\,dA. \] By @lem-gradient-perturbation, \(\|b_1\|_{L^\infty}\le C\) and, from the \(C^1\) remainder used in its proof, \(\|R_1\|_{L^\infty}\le CS\) for \(R_1=|\nabla v|^4-a-tb_1\). Expanding the weighted integral, using the vanishing radial pairing, and applying Cauchy–Schwarz gives \[ \begin{aligned} \int_{\mathbb D}|\nabla v|^4|1+k|^2\,dA &\ge \int_{\mathbb D}a\,dA+\int_{\mathbb D}a|k|^2\,dA\\ &\quad-C\bigl(\sqrt S\sqrt T+\sqrt S\,T+S+S\sqrt T+ST\bigr). \end{aligned} \] The first two errors come from \(t b_1(2\operatorname{Re}k+|k|^2)\), and the remaining ones from \(R_1(1+2\operatorname{Re}k+|k|^2)\). results.proof_text: By @def-conformal-data, \(1+g\) is analytic and nonzero in \(\mathbb D\) with value \(1\) at the origin, so let \(L\) be the analytic logarithm normalized by \(L(0)=0\). Then \(1+g=e^L\) and \((1+g)^{-1}=1+k=e^{-L}\), and the pointwise identity \[ |1+g|^2+|1+k|^2-2 =2\cosh(2\operatorname{Re}L)-2 \ge4(\operatorname{Re}L)^2 \] holds. Integrating and using the definitions of \(S,T\) gives \[ S+T\ge4\|\operatorname{Re}L\|_{A^2}^2. \] The constant coefficient of \(L\) is zero because \((1+g)(0)=1\). For an analytic function with zero constant coefficient, Parseval gives equal Bergman energies for its real and imaginary parts, so \(\|L\|_{A^2}^2=2\|\operatorname{Re}L\|_{A^2}^2\). results.proof_text: Use the similarity invariance in @def-j-functional to normalize \(A(P)=\pi\) and translate so that the Fraenkel-optimal comparison disk is \(D=B_1(0)\). The regular-polygon asymptotic is \[ \frac{J(R_M)}{\pi j^2}=1+\frac{4\zeta(3)}{M^3}+O(M^{-5}). \] The upper bound and the displayed asymptotic give \(\lambda_1(P)\le j^2(1+CN^{-3})\), while Faber–Krahn gives \(\lambda_1(P)\ge j^2\). Quantitative Faber–Krahn therefore gives \(|P\triangle D|\to0\). Let \(u_N\) be the normalized positive eigenfunction and extend it by zero. By @lem-uniform-w14, the extensions are uniformly bounded in \(W^{1,4}(\mathbb R^2)\) and hence equicontinuous and uniformly bounded. Arzelà–Ascoli gives a locally uniform limit along a subsequence. On every compact set outside \(\overline D\), the limit must vanish: otherwise the uniform Hölder bound would force a fixed positive amount of area in \(P_N\setminus D\), contradicting \(|P_N\triangle D|\to0\). The same argument gives zero trace on \(\partial D\). Since \(\|u_N\|_\infty\) is uniformly bounded, the mass outside \(D\) tends to zero; hence the limit has \(L^2(D)\) norm one. Weak lower semicontinuity gives \(\int_D|\nabla u|^2\le\liminf\lambda_1(P_N)=j^2\), while the disk Rayleigh inequality gives the reverse inequality. Thus the limit is the normalized positive disk eigenfunction \(u_0\). Uniqueness of the limit upgrades the whole sequence to local uniform convergence, and the boundary Hölder bound upgrades it to uniform convergence on \(\overline D\). Since \(u_0>0\) on \(B_{1-\eta}\), eventually \(u_N>0\) there; because the zero extension vanishes off \(P_N\), \(B_{1-\eta}\subset P_N\).The maximal conformal radius is at least \(1-\eta\) by monotonicity under inclusion and at most \(1\) by the conformal area inequality \(A(P)\ge\pi r_P^2\). In the normalization of @def-conformal-data, \(1+S=r_P^{-2}\to1\).By @lem-disk-perturbation, once \(N\) is large enough that \(S\le S_0\), the uniform expansion and coercivity give \[ \frac{J(P)}{\pi j^2}-1\ge S/6. \] The regular-polygon upper bound is \(O(N^{-3})\), hence \(S\le CN^{-3}\) with a universal constant.

Differentiating the real part of this formula gives \[ (\log h)'=bx+C_*+\sum_j\frac{a_j(1+x_j^2)}{x-x_j}, \qquad C_*:=\sum_ja_jx_j. \] If \(C_*\ge0\), choose the first edge to the right of \(0\); its parameter interval lies in \((0,\theta_1)\), so \(x>0\) and \(x>x_j\) for every positive prevertex. If \(C_*<0\), choose the last edge to the left; its interval lies in \((\theta_p,2\pi)\), so \(x<0\) and \(x<x_j\) for every positive prevertex. Thus all terms have one sign. Reverse orientation if needed so \(h\) decreases. If the selected edge has parameter length \(\varepsilon\), its positive endpoint has weight \(a\). On its central subarc \([\varepsilon/4,3\varepsilon/4]\), the endpoint term is \[ \frac{1+\cot^2(\varepsilon/2)}{\cot(\theta/2)-\cot(\varepsilon/2)} =\frac{\sin(\theta/2)}{\sin(\varepsilon/2)\sin((\varepsilon-\theta)/2)}\ge c/\varepsilon. \] The negative atom contributes the same lower bound with \(b\); integrating over the central half gives the stated logarithmic drop.
results.statement_text: Suppose the turn measure in @def-turn-measure has exactly one negative atom \(-b\) at \(0\), with \(0<b<1/2\), and let \(a\) be the turn weight at one of the two adjacent positive vertices. There is a choice of one adjacent edge on which \(h=|F'|\) is monotone and, after orienting it decreasingly, \[ \log h(\theta_-)-\log h(\theta_+)\ge c(a+b) \] on a central half of the edge.

results.proof_text: By @def-conformal-data, \(r_{R_M}\) denotes the conformal-radius function used in the normalization. We use the standard theorem that the conformal-radius function of a bounded convex planar domain is concave. The regular polygon is convex and invariant under the rotations \(\sigma_k(z)=e^{2\pi ik/M}z\). For every \(z\) in the polygon, \[ 0=\frac1M\sum_{k=0}^{M-1}\sigma_k(z). \] Concavity and rotational invariance give \[ r_{R_M}(0)\ge\frac1M\sum_{k=0}^{M-1}r_{R_M}(\sigma_kz)=r_{R_M}(z). \] Thus the center is a maximizer. Uniqueness of the centered Riemann map after fixing \(F_M'(0)>0\) and equivariance under the rotation group imply \(F_M(e^{2\pi i/M}z)=e^{2\pi i/M}F_M(z)\); differentiating twice at \(0\) gives \(F_M''(0)=0\).
results.statement_text: For a regular \(M\)-gon \(R_M\), the center is a point where the maximal conformal radius in @def-conformal-data is attained. Consequently the similarity-normalized Riemann map may be chosen centered at the center of \(R_M\) and satisfies \(F_M''(0)=0\).

The regular \(M\)-gon is invariant under rotations about its center, and its Schwarz–Christoffel derivative is \[ F_M'(z)=(1-z^M)^{-2/M}=1+g_M(z),qquad g_M(z)=\sum_{q\ge1}c_qz^{qM},qquad c_q=\frac{(2/M)_q}{q!}. \] By @lem-regular-sc-coefficient-sum and @def-conformal-data, \[ S_M=\sum_{q\ge1}\frac{c_q^2}{qM+1} =\frac{4\zeta(3)}{M^3}+O(M^{-5}). \]Apply @lem-disk-perturbation to \(g_M\). The quadratic correction satisfies \[ \left|\sum_{q\ge1}\frac{\rho_{qM}}{(qM+1)^2}c_q^2\right| \le \frac{C}{M^2}\sum_{q\ge1}\frac{c_q^2}{qM+1}=O(M^{-5}), \] using @lem-bessel-ratio-decay. Since \(S_M=O(M^{-3})\), it is below the fixed perturbation threshold for all sufficiently large \(M\), and \(S_M^{3/2}=O(M^{-9/2})\). The perturbation expansion yields \[ \frac{J(R_M)}{\pi j^2}=1+\frac{4\zeta(3)}{M^3}+O(M^{-9/2}). \]

results.proof_text: Write \[ c_q=\frac\alpha qP_q, \qquad P_q=\prod_{r=1}^{q-1}\left(1+\frac\alpha r\right), \qquad H_q=\sum_{r=1}^q\frac1r. \] Set \(Q=\lfloor e^{1/(4\alpha)}\rfloor\). For \(q\le Q\), \(\alpha H_{q-1}\le1/2\) and the product expansion with a positive remainder gives \[ P_q=1+\alpha H_{q-1}+R_q, \qquad |R_q|\le C\alpha^2(1+H_{q-1}^2). \] Also \[ \frac1{qM+1}=\frac1{qM}-\frac1{q^2M^2}+O\left(\frac1{q^3M^3}\right). \] Substitution, using convergence of \(\sum q^{-3}\), \(\sum H_{q-1}q^{-3}\) and \(\sum(1+H_{q-1}^2)q^{-3}\), gives \[ \sum_{q\le Q}\frac{c_q^2}{qM+1} =\frac{\alpha^2}{M}\zeta(3) +\frac{2\alpha^3}{M}\sum_{q\ge1}\frac{H_{q-1}}{q^3} -\frac{\alpha^2}{M^2}\zeta(4)+O(M^{-5}). \] The standard Euler sum \(\sum_{q\ge1}H_{q-1}/q^3=\zeta(4)/4\) and \(\alpha=2/M\) make the two \(M^{-4}\) terms cancel, leaving \(4\zeta(3)M^{-3}+O(M^{-5})\).For \(q>Q\), the Gamma-ratio estimate \(P_q\le Cq^\alpha\) gives \[ \sum_{q>Q}\frac{c_q^2}{qM+1} \le\frac{C\alpha^2}{M}\sum_{q>Q}q^{-3+2\alpha} \le C M^{-3}e^{-1/(2\alpha)}=O(M^{-5}). \] This proves the claim.

results.proof_text: The first-order perturbation and the second-order disk calculation from @lem-disk-perturbation give \[ \frac{J(P)}{\pi j^2}=1+S-\sum_{n\ge2}\frac{\rho_n}{(n+1)^2}|g_n|^2+O(S^{3/2}), \] with \(\beta_n=n+1-\rho_n\). By @lem-gradient-perturbation, @lem-inverse-energy and @lem-airy-quadratic-response, \[ S-T=2\sum_{n\ge2}\frac{\beta_n^2}{(n+1)^2(n^2-1)}|g_n|^2+O\bigl(S^{3/2}\sqrt{\log(e/S)}\bigr). \] By @lem-log-energy-bound, \(\|L\|_{A^2}^2\le(S+T)/2\), and by @lem-frequency-replacement every quadratic form with multiplier \(O((n+1)^{-2})\) may replace \(g\) by \(L\) at an error of order \(S^{3/2}\sqrt{\log(e/S)}\). Combining these facts with the scalar expansion gives Put \(d_n=\beta_n^2/((n+1)^2(n^2-1))\), \(r_n=\rho_n/(n+1)^2\), and \(E=S^{3/2}\sqrt{\log(e/S)}\). The Airy response gives \(T=S-2\sum d_n|g_n|^2+O(E)\), so the logarithmic bound gives \[ S\ge \|L\|_{A^2}^2+\sum_{n\ge2}d_n|g_n|^2-O(E). \] The scalar disk expansion therefore yields \[ \frac{J(P)}{\pi j^2} \ge1+\|L\|_{A^2}^2+\sum_{n\ge2}(d_n-r_n)|g_n|^2-O(E). \] Since \(0<\rho_n<2\) and \(0<\beta_n<n+1\), one has \[ |d_n-r_n|\le\frac{C}{(n+1)^2}. \] Thus @lem-frequency-replacement changes the last quadratic form from \(g\) to \(L\) at cost \(O(E)\). Since \(L(0)=L_1=0\), Bergman Parseval gives \(\|L\|_{A^2}^2=\sum_{n\ge2}|L_n|^2/(n+1)\), and \[ \frac1{n+1}+d_n-r_n =\frac{\beta_n}{(n+1)^2}\left(1+\frac{\beta_n}{n^2-1}\right). \] Finally, @def-turn-measure gives \(L_n=2\widehat\mu(n)/n\), so the coefficient becomes \(4a_n\) and the claimed inequality follows after shrinking \(S_0\) to absorb the \(O(S^{3/2})\) term into \(O(E)\). \[ \frac{J(P)}{\pi j^2}\ge1+\sum_{n\ge2}\frac{\beta_n}{(n+1)^2}\left(1+\frac{\beta_n}{n^2-1}\right)|L_n|^2-C S^{3/2}\sqrt{\log(e/S)}. \] Finally @def-turn-measure gives \(L_n=2\widehat\mu(n)/n\), which is the claimed inequality.

results.proof_text: Define on \(\ell^2(\mathbb N_0)\) the self-adjoint matrix \[ A_{rs}=\tau^{(r+s)/2}\widehat\mu(r-s)=\sum_iw_i(v_i)_r\overline{(v_i)_s}, \qquad (v_i)_r=\tau^{r/2}e^{-ir\theta_i}. \] The Vandermonde vectors at distinct nodes are linearly independent, so \(A\) has exactly \(p\) positive eigenvalues \(\alpha_1\ge\cdots\ge\alpha_p>0\). The trace is \((1-\tau)^{-1}\), and the negative eigenvalues can only decrease the trace, hence \(Q:=\sum_i\alpha_i\ge(1-\tau)^{-1}\). The shift compression and the min–max principle give \(\alpha_{i+1}\le\tau\alpha_i\). For fixed \(Q\) and these ratio constraints, a finite exchange argument (move mass from an earlier coordinate to the latest coordinate until the active constraint is met) shows that the minimum of the strictly convex function \(\sum_i\alpha_i^2\) is attained at \[ \alpha_i=Q\frac{(1-\tau)\tau^{i-1}}{1-\tau^p},\qquad 1\le i\le p. \] Consequently \[ \sum_i\alpha_i^2\ge Q^2\frac{1-\tau}{1+\tau}\frac{1+\tau^p}{1-\tau^p} \ge\frac{1+\tau^p}{(1-\tau^2)(1-\tau^p)}. \] On the other hand, \[ \|A\|_{HS}^2=\frac{1+2\sum_{n\ge1}\tau^n|\widehat\mu(n)|^2}{1-\tau^2} \] and the Hilbert–Schmidt norm dominates the squared positive eigenvalues. Rearranging gives \[ 1+2\sum_{n\ge1}\tau^n|\widehat\mu(n)|^2\ge\frac{1+\tau^p}{1-\tau^p}, \] which is exactly the claimed bound.

results.proof_text: The domain-independent Dirichlet heat-kernel estimate gives \(\|u\|_\infty^2\le e^2\lambda/(8\pi)\) for the normalized first eigenfunction. Under the edge-moment hypotheses, @lem-airy-identity applies, and \(\int_Pu^4\le\|u\|_\infty^2\int_Pu^2=\|u\|_\infty^2\); combining these facts yields \[ \int_P|\nabla u|^4\le \frac{e^2\lambda^3}{8\pi}. \] The same \(L^\infty\) bound gives \(\int_P|u|^4\le\|u\|_\infty^2\), so the \(W^{1,4}(P)\) norm is bounded by a constant depending only on \(A_0\) and \(\Lambda\). results.proof_text: By @def-conformal-data, \(g\) has no constant coefficient, so \(h\) has no constant coefficient when \(S>0\). Write \(g=th\), \(t=\sqrt S\), and \(\|h\|_{A^2}=1\). By @lem-c1-perturbation, \[ v=v_0+t v_1+e, \qquad \|e\|_{L^\infty(\mathbb D)}\le CS, \qquad \|v_1\|_{L^\infty(\mathbb D)}\le C, \] and \(v_1\) has no radial Fourier mode. By @lem-disk-perturbation, \(|\lambda-j^2|\le CS\). Since \(v_0\) is radial and \(h\) has no constant coefficient, angular orthogonality gives \[ \int_{\mathbb D}v_0^3v_1\,dA=0, \qquad \int_{\mathbb D}v_0^4\operatorname{Re}h\,dA=0. \] The boundedness of \(v_0,v_1,e\) and Cauchy–Schwarz imply \[ v^4=v_0^4+4t v_0^3v_1+E, \qquad \|E\|_{L^\infty(\mathbb D)}\le CS. \] Multiplying by \(|1+th|^2=1+2t\operatorname{Re}h+t^2|h|^2\) and using \(\|h\|_{L^1}\le C\|h\|_{A^2}\) gives \[ \left|\int_{\mathbb D}v^4|1+g|^2\,dA-\int_{\mathbb D}v_0^4\,dA\right|\le CS. \] Indeed the only terms of order \(t\) are the two displayed zero integrals; all remaining terms contain either \(E\), \(t^2|h|^2\), or the product \(t^2v_0^3v_1\operatorname{Re}h\) and are \(O(S)\). Therefore \[ \lambda^2\int_{\mathbb D}v^4|1+g|^2\,dA =j^4\int_{\mathbb D}v_0^4\,dA+O(S), \qquad \frac{\lambda^2}{\pi(1+S)}=\frac{j^4}{\pi}+O(S). \] The radial Bessel equation for \(v_0\), integrated by parts using \(v_0(1)=0\) and \(\int_{\mathbb D}v_0^2dA=1\), gives \[ \int_{\mathbb D}|\nabla v_0|^4\,dA =j^4\left(\int_{\mathbb D}v_0^4\,dA-\frac1\pi\right). \] Combining these displays proves the claim.
results.statement_text: For normalized conformal data in @def-conformal-data with \(S\) sufficiently small, let \(v\) and \(\lambda\) be the positive weighted first eigenpair in @lem-disk-perturbation, and let \(v_0(r)=J_0(jr)/(\sqrt\pi J_1(j))\). Then \[ \left|\lambda^2\int_{\mathbb D}v^4|1+g|^2\,dA- \frac{\lambda^2}{\pi(1+S)}- \int_{\mathbb D}|\nabla v_0|^4\,dA\right|\le CS. \] The constant is universal.
